finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto the authenticated user object and persists it. Any user can set privileged or identity fields such as role, isAdmin, id, email, or password hash, which allows privilege escalation or account takeover. This assumes the user model holds such fields; that is not visible in this file.
finding.source: req.body: attacker-controlled JSON from any authenticated user

trace.note: PUT /me handler; the only visible control is whatever middleware populates req.user
Object.assign merges all attacker-supplied keys into the user record with no allowlist
The full user object is returned, so the change can be confirmed and internal fields are exposed

finding.guards_checked: No field allowlist or schema validation in this file. The sibling route /me/profile destructures only displayName and bio, which shows the intended safe pattern and that /me bypasses it. Auth and user-model middleware are not in this directory, so I could not check them. Object.assign onto a plain object does not pollute Object.prototype, because __proto__ in parsed JSON is an own property and the assignment does not recurse.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation, then users.js:6 saves it and users.js:7 returns it, so any authenticated user can write arbitrary fields. The sibling route at users.js:11 destructures only displayName and bio, which shows the safe pattern. Whether the user model has privileged fields can't be seen, since users.js is the only file here.

verdict_facts.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist, schema or role check, and users.js:6 saves the result, so any user who can reach PUT /me can overwrite any field of their own record. This is unlike the allowlisted /me/profile route at users.js:11-12. Whether the user model has privileged fields can't be seen in this directory, but the missing control is real.
